subject: The Intelligent Investor: Don't Let Politics Poison Your Portfolio

96 Plus, not much FOMO on private markets.   Is this email difficult to read? A ratty-looking street vendor tries to sell rat poison to a skeptical homeowner. The peddler, who purports to be able to kill rodents, has one perched nonchalantly on his shoulder, while another rat watches from the top of the peddler’s basket. MINNEAPOLIS INSTITUTE OF ART   Fellow investors,

   Election Day in the U.S. is a week from today, while Brazil and Israel, among other countries, have also been holding national polls.

   It’s a perfect time for me to remind you: For investors, politics is mental poison. Express your political opinions at your polling place or by volunteering or, if you must, by hollering at your relatives during Thanksgiving dinner. But please keep your politics out of your investing forecasts.

   To see why that’s so important, just look at this chart, from a recent paper by University of Arizona finance professor Rick Sias and colleagues:

     Average probability the stock market will rise over the coming year “POLITICAL POLARIZATION AND STOCK MARKET EXPECTATIONS,” SSRN.COM   Based on a sample of more than 12,000 Americans who participated in surveys between 2015 and 2025, the chart tracks the views of those who identify most intensely as either Republicans or Democrats. The surveys asked how likely the stock market was to rise over the next 12 months. The blue dotted line shows the Democratic average; the red line, the Republican average.

   As you can see, when a Democrat was in the White House, Democrats thought the stock market was more likely to do well over the coming year. When a Republican became president, Democrats downgraded their expectations. Republicans did the exact opposite.

   What’s striking is how partisan people are when they predict stock returns. Republicans and Democrats alike flip their forecasts right after presidential elections. (Partisans also “maintain their polarized equity return perceptions” after midterm elections, the researchers find.)

   If you’re a Republican who lightened up on stocks when Biden won, or a Democrat who sold stocks when Trump won, you let your political preferences shape your investments—and shot yourself in the foot. Stocks crashed in early 2020 under Trump and had a bad year in 2022 under Biden. But, overall, they did well under both presidents.

   U.S. stocks have delivered positive real returns in about 70% of all one-year periods since 1793, according to financial historian Edward McQuarrie. Under Republican presidents, the stock market has boomed (the Roaring 1920s, much of the 1950s, 1982-87) and tanked (1929-32, 1974-75, 2001-02). Under Democratic presidents, the stock market has boomed (1942-45, 1995-99, 2009-14) and tanked (1937, much of the 1960s, 2000). Which party controls Congress (or Congress and the White House) doesn’t reliably forecast returns, either.

   Rick Sias, one of the researchers behind the recent study, warns that these polarized forecasts “appear larger among more-numerate and financially literate investors.” He adds, “the people best equipped to form accurate views appear to distort their judgment the most.”

   Hasn’t politics become nasty and hateful enough without letting it contaminate your investing decisions? Your vote belongs in the ballot box, not in your portfolio.

   This is an edition of the Intelligent Investor newsletter, where Jason Zweig writes twice monthly about investment strategy and how to think about money. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

           No FOMO Here   In the last issue , I asked:

   My last column, “ Private Equity Has a Problem. Uncle Sam Says Your Wallet Can Fix It ,” looked at new rule proposals from the SEC that would make it easier for private funds to market to the investing public. The managers of funds offering private equity, private credit, nontraded real estate and other alternative assets [or ”alts”] say it isn’t fair that pension funds and university endowments have access to such funds while small investors don’t. Do you think it’s unfair?

   Here’s a sample of opinions:

   Offering alts to retail investors is not a matter of fairness. It is a matter of survival for the offer-ers.
 —Steven Adler, California 

   What the managers of funds offering private equity, private credit, non-traded real estate and other alternative assets are really saying is that it isn’t fair that they don’t have access to the huge sum of small investors’ aggregate funds. Adding more capital to chase the same number of deals will only reduce the returns further. Letting people who have no cushion in life invest in these assets is not only foolish, but cruel.
 —Philip L. Fitting, Rhode Island 

   The best private funds are an access class. Those with access to the very best funds earn above market returns. The very best funds are disciplined. They usually keep their funds small to keep the quality high. Too much money chasing the same opportunity set depresses returns. The SEC proposal will allow the investing public the freedom to lose their money and learn a valuable lesson along the way.
 — Steve McMenamin , Connecticut 

   We are still trying to get a couple of clients out of investments they made with prior advisers that promised the moon but have failed to deliver. We are stuck each quarter navigating the redemption process for each fund and hoping we can get out. If financial-planning firms such as ours cannot get comfortable, how is a normal investor going to know how to understand what they’re buying?
 —Stacey Hyde, Tennessee 

   I don’t think access to private equity or debt is a matter of fairness for small investors: It is a matter of liquidity and deep pockets. The ability to go years without access to your money is a huge risk that even sophisticated / institutional investors underestimate.
 —William Pardee, Virginia 

   Public pension plans are invested to the gills in this stuff, and [that] financial exposure already rests with the public. In presenting [alternative] investments to clients, maybe financial advisers should be required to quantify the pass-through from public pension plans as the baseline to which new investment exposures would be added.
 — Larry Pollack   

       Catching Up   My latest columns:

   Brokerage Firms Want to Yank Away Your Investor Protections explains how arbitration over financial losses might soon get harder than it already is.
 Your Cheap ETF Costs More Than You Think looks at why some of the world’s biggest ETFs charge higher fees than they probably need to.

       The WSJ Wayback Machine   Almost exactly 70 years ago, in October 1956, The Wall Street Journal ran this article on Page One:

     The Wall Street Journal, Oct. 19, 1956, p. 1   “TV phones” did catch on—almost 65 years later, as I wrote in late 2020 , amid the boom in Zoom calls during the pandemic.

   As if the nuclear-powered internal radio network weren’t enough, the story also predicted:

     WSJ, Oct. 19, 1956.   Given this week’s hype over the pending IPO by Anthropic , this look back in time should remind us all to be skeptical of grandiose technological predictions. New technologies often change the world even more than their wildest proponents predict—but the changes are often slower, more diffuse and applied in more unusual ways than anyone expected. And the most improbable companies are sometimes the ultimate winners.

       Question of the Week   And that brings us to what must be the question of the week: Amid all the hype about giant IPOs like Anthropic and OpenAI, what do you think people are getting wrong? When we look back on AI five or 10 years from now, what will seem obvious then that many investors seem to be missing now? What might be the biggest surprises in how the AI industry develops, and which investments could pay off the best—and worst? 

   Share your thoughts in the comments or, if you’re reading this as an email, just hit reply. Please include your name and location. Responses may be lightly edited for clarity and brevity.

       Clarification   In the last issue, I said the new publication “ Exponential Wealth ,” an outstanding presentation of the long-term returns of stock, bonds and other assets, is published by the CFA Institute. It’s published by an affiliate, the CFA Institute Research Foundation.

       Money Mailbag   Have a question you’d like me to answer?

   Want to weigh in on what you just read? Got a tip on something that I or my colleagues should investigate? Itching to tell me I’m wrong about something?

   Just email intelligentinvestor@wsj.com and I’ll see your note. Don’t forget to include your name and city.

   Be well and invest well,

   Jason

Given this week’s hype over the pending IPO by Anthropic, this look back in time should remind us all to be skeptical of grandiose technological predictions.
